period.label: About AD 60-62
period.note: This follows the traditional view that Paul wrote from Rome. If he wrote from Ephesus (about AD 54-55) or Caesarea (about AD 57-59), Nero was still emperor and the setting is much the same.

rulers.name: Nero
rulers.text: Emperor over Rome, Asia and Judea. Paul, a Roman citizen, had appealed to Caesar, who in these years was Nero.

rulers.name: The proconsul of Asia
rulers.role: Governor of the province where Colossae stood
rulers.text: Asia was governed by a proconsul appointed for a year at a time, who heard cases in the province's leading cities.

rulers.name: Festus and Agrippa II
rulers.role: Governor of Judea and Jewish client king
rulers.text: Festus and King Agrippa heard Paul's defense in Caesarea and sent him on to Rome as he had asked.

events.title: Rome and Parthia fight over Armenia
events.text: Roman armies under Corbulo campaigned in Armenia until the two empires made peace in AD 63.

events.title: Paul's voyage to Rome
events.text: Paul sailed for Rome as a prisoner, was shipwrecked on Malta, and reached Rome the following spring.

events.title: Earthquake in the Lycus valley
events.text: An earthquake ruined Laodicea, about 16 km (10 miles) from Colossae; Laodicea rebuilt without Rome's help. A later Christian historian says Hierapolis and Colossae fell in the same disaster.

events.title: Boudica's revolt in Britain
events.text: Boudica, queen of the Iceni, led a rising that burned Colchester, London and St Albans before the Romans defeated her.

events.title: Paul under guard in Rome
events.text: Paul lived two whole years in his own rented house, guarded by a soldier, receiving all who came to him. Colossians, Philemon, Ephesians and Philippians are traditionally dated to these years.

events.title: A slave-owner's murder shakes Rome
events.text: When the city prefect Pedanius Secundus was killed by one of his slaves, the Senate upheld the old law that all 400 slaves of his household be executed, despite protests from the crowd.

events.title: James, the Lord's brother, is killed
events.text: Between governors, the high priest Ananus had "James, the brother of Jesus who was called Christ" stoned in Jerusalem.

events.title: Fire in Rome, and Nero blames the Christians
events.text: After a great fire burned much of Rome, Nero blamed the Christians and put a "vast multitude" to death.

places.name: Colossae
places.summary: Where Philemon and the church in his house lived. A small town in the Lycus valley of Phrygia, in the Roman province of Asia, about 190 km (120 miles) east of Ephesus.

facts.text: Colossae stood near Laodicea and Hierapolis. Paul names believers in all three, and the letters to Colossae and Laodicea were to be swapped and read in both churches.

facts.topic: An old city past its prime
facts.text: The Greek historian Herodotus called Colossae "a great city of Phrygia" in the 400s BC. By Paul's day nearby Laodicea had outgrown it; Strabo lists it only as a small town.
The valley was known for its wool. Pliny mentions a dye color named after Colossae, colossinus, a reddish purple.
Paul had not visited it himself. Epaphras, a Colossian, first taught the gospel there, and the church met in homes such as Philemon's.

places.name: Rome
places.summary: Where Paul wrote from, on the traditional view: the capital of the empire, where he waited under guard to be heard by Caesar.

facts.topic: A prisoner in his own house
facts.text: Paul was allowed to live by himself with a soldier guarding him, bound with a chain, yet free to receive visitors and preach.
The same people send greetings in Philemon and Colossians: Epaphras, Mark, Aristarchus, Demas and Luke.

life.text: Slaves served in households of every size, as laborers, servants, stewards and teachers, and many were later freed. Roman law gave a master almost complete power over a slave. Paul's letters address believing slaves and masters directly.
Onesimus was a common name for slaves and means "useful" or "profitable." Paul plays on it: once unprofitable, now profitable.

Roman lawyers discussed slaves who went to a friend of their master to ask him to plead for them, and held that such a slave was not counted a runaway. Pliny the Younger wrote a letter of this kind, begging a friend to forgive a freedman who had come to him in tears.
Christians had no church buildings yet. They met in the homes of believers who had room to host them.
Paul usually dictated his letters to a scribe and wrote a line or two himself as his mark.
Travellers preferred to stay with friends rather than at inns. Paul asks Philemon to get a room ready, hoping to be released.

basis: Scripture first, then ancient writers on these years and places (Tacitus, Suetonius, Josephus, Strabo, Herodotus, Pliny, Roman law). Drafted by Claude and not yet reviewed by a person.
